introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of two books open before us, the Book of Creation and the Book of Revelation, and of two sides to everything human: body and spirit, material and divine civilization, the food, happiness, music, kinship, leadership and life that belong to each. These hundred passages go through those pairs. They value the material and still rank it second, as the lower floor of a house one does not leave by going upstairs. Beside them are a hundred voices from elsewhere: the Gospels and Paul, the Psalms and the Qur’an, Plato, Seneca and Pascal, Browne, Wordsworth, Thoreau and Emerson, with Whitman and Blake speaking for the body, and Khayyam, Lucretius, Marx and Machiavelli for this world alone.
questions: "When you go upstairs in a house you do not leave the house." How does that image answer Whitman, who will not rank body below soul, and Blake, who denies they are two?
Thomas Browne and Psalm 19 also read two books. What can each book say that the other cannot?
One passage says material happiness never exists. What would FitzGerald's Omar reply, and what would you say to him?
Several letters say that distance of body does not matter between friends, and one talk that "the ties of the flesh are nothing." How does David's grief for Absalom bear on that?
Europe is called a beautiful body without a spirit. Wordsworth, Emerson and Arnold said similar things of their own age. What would it mean for a civilization to have a spirit?
Machiavelli held that unarmed prophets fail. What kind of power do the last passages describe, and how has it fared?

outside.why: Thomas Browne wrote that he drew his divinity from two books: the written one of God, and nature, the public manuscript open to all eyes.
The psalm that begins with the heavens declaring God's glory turns in its second half to the law that restores the soul: both books in one song.
Thoreau says that castles in the air need not be lost; the task is to put foundations under them.
Kant names two things that fill the mind with awe, one outside him and one within.
Jesus says that man shall not live by bread alone. This passage adds that the body still needs its bread. How are the two sayings to be held together?
Emerson holds that every natural fact is a symbol of some spiritual fact, which makes the world a book.
This is the verse quoted: an oath by the pen and by what is written with it.
Paul calls his converts a letter written not with ink but by the Spirit, on tablets of the heart.
Bacon judged that a little philosophy inclines the mind to atheism and depth in philosophy brings it round to religion.
Plato divides what is into the visible and the intelligible, each with its own source of light.
Paul says that what is prepared has not been seen or heard or imagined.
Plato likens the visible world to shadows thrown on a cave wall by a light the prisoners have not seen.
Paul says that the invisible things are understood from the things that are made.
Paul tells the Colossians to set their affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
Lovelace wrote from prison that stone walls do not make one for a mind that is free.
The Qur’an names God the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward together.
Pope sets man on an isthmus between two worlds, belonging to both.
Whitman announces himself the poet of the body and the poet of the soul, and refuses to rank them. How does caring for "man's two natures" differ from his equal praise?
Paul speaks of the body as an earthly tent, and of a house not made with hands.
The Preacher says that the dust returns to the earth and the spirit to God who gave it.
Bacon saw that knowledge of the causes in nature gives power over nature, which is how it becomes a servant.
A psalm marvels that man is given dominion over the works of God's hands.
Pascal calls man a reed, the weakest thing in nature, whose whole dignity is thought.
Paul says that though the outward man perishes, the inward man is renewed day by day.
Milton defined the end of learning as knowing God aright and growing like him.
Plato describes education as turning the whole soul toward the light, not filling it.
Whitman grew tired of the astronomer's proofs and went out to look at the stars in silence. Is that the limit of material science described here, or something else?
Jesus tells his disciples that he has food to eat of which they know nothing.
Jesus says to labour not for the food that perishes but for the food that endures.
The first Christians broke bread from house to house with gladness and singleness of heart.
Seneca says that it is not the man who has little but the man who craves more who is poor.
Jesus warns that a life does not consist in the abundance of things possessed.
The Preacher tried every pleasure and labour and found it vanity and a striving after wind.
FitzGerald's Omar asks for a loaf, a jug of wine, a book of verse and a companion, and calls that paradise enough. What would he say to the claim that material happiness never exists?
Mill held that it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied.
Jesus asks what it profits a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul.
Thoreau reckoned a man rich in proportion to the number of things he can afford to let alone.
Habakkuk rejoices in God though the fig tree does not blossom and the stalls are empty.
Paul says that the things which are seen are temporal, and the things not seen are eternal.
Arnold heard in his own century the sea of faith withdrawing down the shingles of the world.
Wordsworth laments that in getting and spending we lay waste our powers and have given our hearts away.
Jesus says that where a person's treasure is, the heart will be also.
Thoreau observed that the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
Plato's Socrates describes the soul as looking at the world through the bars of a prison.
Blake denies that man has a body distinct from his soul: the body is the portion of soul the senses discern. What is lost if the body is thought of only as a cage?
A psalm sings of the soul escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers.
Huxley argued that ethical progress means combating the struggle for existence, not imitating it. Does a struggle "in the world of the spirit" continue nature's law or reverse it?
Paul contrasts the mind set on the flesh, which is death, with the mind set on the Spirit, which is life and peace.
Paul says that flesh and Spirit desire against each other, so that a person cannot simply do as he would.
Tennyson calls on his reader to move upward, working out the beast.
Jesus tells Nicodemus that what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Paul says that now we see in a mirror, dimly, and know in part.
Jesus tells his disciples that in his Father's house are many mansions, and that he goes to prepare a place.
The first letter of John says that the world passes away, and its desire with it.
Lucretius argued that death is nothing to us, as the ages before our birth were nothing. If he is right, what becomes of the comparison made here?
This is the saying of Jesus that the passage quotes: let the dead bury their dead.
Jesus says that he came so that people might have life, and have it more abundantly.
The Qur’an calls the life of the world play and pageantry, like growth after rain that soon turns to straw.
Jesus says that foxes have holes and birds have nests, but he has nowhere to lay his head.
Paul tells the Philippians that their citizenship is in heaven, whatever city they live in.
Isaiah promises that those who wait on the Lord shall mount up with wings as eagles.
Paul writes to the Colossians that he is absent in the flesh and with them in the spirit.
Paul tells the Thessalonians that he was taken from them in presence, not in heart.
Peter writes to people who love one they have never seen, and rejoice in him.
Donne tells his wife that two souls which are one suffer no breach when the bodies part.
Samuel was told that man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart.
Jesus says that whoever does the will of his Father is his brother and sister and mother.
David's cry for his dead son Absalom shows what the ties of the flesh can be. Are they "nothing," or do they only yield to something greater?
John's Gospel speaks of children born not of blood or of the will of the flesh, but of God.
This is the elder brother's complaint in the parable, and the father's answer.
Plato held that rhythm and harmony find their way into the inner places of the soul.
Pope calls all nature art unknown to us, and all discord harmony not understood.
Paul asks for psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, sung with grace in the heart.
This is the verse quoted: are those who know equal with those who know not?
Jesus tells Martha that one thing is needful, and that Mary has chosen it.
Herbert asks to see God in all things and to do every task as for him, which makes drudgery divine.
Paul says: whatever you do, do it heartily, as to the Lord.
Jesus says that people are known by their fruits, as a tree is: deeds are the picture that shows.
Jesus says that it is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing.
Paul tells the Ephesians that they have been made alive by grace.
Emerson put the danger in eight words: things are in the saddle, and ride mankind.
Jesus tells of a man who laid up goods for many years and was not rich toward God.
Tagore prays for a country where knowledge is free and the mind is led forward into ever-widening thought and action.
Ezekiel saw bodies fully formed, with sinews and flesh and skin, that did not live until breath came into them.
Paul says that the letter kills and the spirit gives life, in religion as in a civilization.
Arnold felt his Europe wandering between two worlds, one dead and the other powerless to be born. Is that the body without a spirit described here?
Thoreau went to the woods to front the essential facts of life, and not discover at death that he had not lived.
Marx called religion the sigh of the oppressed creature and the opium of the people, and looked to material change. What does this talk say that material fraternity cannot do?
A psalm says that unless the Lord builds the house, they labour in vain who build it.
Jesus says to seek first the kingdom of God, and that the other things will be added.
Gibbon describes a humble religion that grew in silence and at last raised its banner over the ruins of the empire that had persecuted it.
Jesus contrasts the rulers of the nations, who lord it over them, with the greatness of the servant.
Machiavelli advised that a ruler is safer feared than loved. What kind of leadership does this talk have in mind that his rule does not reach?
Jesus tells Pilate that his kingdom is not of this world, or his servants would fight.
Zechariah heard: not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.
Peter had no silver or gold to give the beggar at the gate, and gave him what he had.
Machiavelli observed that armed prophets have conquered and unarmed prophets have been destroyed. How does the history told in these letters answer him?
This is the saying of Jesus about the abomination of desolation that the talk interprets.
The Qur’an says that to God belong the creation and the command, the two realms this prayer names.
A psalm says that the heavens declare the glory of God, the first of the two books.

john-meat-which-perisheth.text: Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life, which the Son of man shall give unto you

john-meat-ye-know-not-of.text: But he said unto them, I have meat to eat that ye know not of. Therefore said the disciples one to another, Hath any man brought him ought to eat? Jesus saith unto them, My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work

corinthians-things-not-seen-are-eternal.text: While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal

philippians-conversation-is-in-heaven.text: For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ

romans-carnally-minded.text: For they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh; but they that are after the Spirit the things of the Spirit. For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace

ecclesiastes-eat-drink-and-be-merry.text: Then I commended mirth, because a man hath no better thing under the sun

matthew-princes-of-the-gentiles.text: But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them. But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister; And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant

galatians-flesh-against-the-spirit.text: This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would

acts-breaking-bread-with-gladness.text: And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart, Praising God, and having favour with all the people

quran-nun-by-the-pen.text: Nun. By the pen and that which they write (therewith),

quran-creation-and-commandment.text: Lo! your Lord is Allah Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days, then mounted He the Throne. He covereth the night with the day, which is in haste to follow it, and hath made the sun and the moon and the stars subservient by His command. His verily is all creation and commandment. Blessed be Allah, the Lord of the Worlds!

whitman-poet-of-the-body.text: I am the poet of the Body and I am the poet of the Soul, / The pleasures of heaven are with me and the pains of hell are with me, / The first I graft and increase upon myself, the latter I translate into a new tongue
whitman-poet-of-the-body.author: Walt Whitman

wordsworth-getting-and-spending.text: The world is too much with us; late and soon, / Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers: / Little we see in Nature that is ours; / We have given our hearts away, a sordid boon
wordsworth-getting-and-spending.author: William Wordsworth
wordsworth-getting-and-spending.work: “The world is too much with us”

blake-no-body-distinct-from-his-soul.text: Man has no Body distinct from his Soul for that called Body is a portion of Soul discernd by the five Senses, the chief inlets of Soul in this age
blake-no-body-distinct-from-his-soul.author: William Blake
blake-no-body-distinct-from-his-soul.work: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell

emerson-things-are-in-the-saddle.text: Things are in the saddle, / And ride mankind
emerson-things-are-in-the-saddle.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
emerson-things-are-in-the-saddle.work: Ode, Inscribed to W. H. Channing

matthew-seek-ye-first.text: But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you
